utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-81-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. May we have the appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it's Lorna Bolton, Mark Harmon, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Bolton. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Daniela Tasic, Chad Mair, Milos Androvic, Kay Marshall, Novak Lukic, and I'm Gregor Guy-Smith on behalf of Mr. Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Before we start, just for the record, we sit in pursuant to Rule 15 bis this afternoon. Judge David is finish in Lukic and Lukic trying to finish up before the other judge leaves the Tribunal. Madam Bolton, will you call your witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Sacirbey, good afternoon or good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. I was looking for a witness in court here, that's why I said call your witness, I forgot you were far away. Mr. Sacirbey, just to remind you that you are still bound by the declaration you made on the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, and I remain close to those words, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It has come to the notice of the Chamber that the room you are in is very warm and that, at some stage, you might prefer to take off your jacket, we will understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour I understand that it's very important to try to get through all the material and give Defence counsel the opportunity for cross, so I have tried to endeavour to go through this even under some rather stuffy conditions here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the interest of justice, I hope you will allow that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If you want to take off your jacket feel free.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going start today by just clarifying a few things that you've said in your testimony to date, and just want to remind you at the outset of the need for you to be succinct in your answers as we have a great deal of material to cover. Okay?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, on the first day of your evidence and this is at page 7148 of the transcript, you referred to something you called UN TV?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What does UN TV broadcast?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I can mostly speak from the time when I was at the United Nations as ambassador. It would tend to have sometimes independent broadcasting including panels, but most critically, I believe to what we have testified to, it would broadcast all the meetings of the UN Security Council and the General Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And when you say all the meetings, are we talking about the public meetings or the private consultations you've discussed or both?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are only speaking of public meetings, and I can only say all to the extent that I am aware. Of course there may be situations that I'm unaware of where that did not occur.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: So did you physically have to be in the either the Security Council Chamber or the General Assembly Chamber to be keeping track of the proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you did not. And frequently, I actually might keep track of these proceedings from my offices, that is the BiH mission to the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Turning to a different issue, sir, when I was asking you questions at page 7149 of the transcript about the arms embargo and -- imposed by Resolution 713, you told us that Bosnia had been deemed to be subject to it, and I neglected to ask if anyone else was also subject to that order?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the entire territory of the former Yugoslavia ultimately was deemed to be subject to it as it was a transitional situation. The first reference was to Yugoslavia. Subsequent references seemed to expand its application to the entire territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. On another issue sir, or related issue, if I could ask you to turn to the binder from 1993, I think will have tab 21 in it. This is 65 ter 8820. Sorry, it's the very last document in that tab that contains several other documents.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Registrar is helping me here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Do you have the document in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It should be a document titled letter dated 22nd April, 1993 from the "Charge d'affair of the Permanent Mission of Yugoslavia," is that the right document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And yesterday in the context of discussing the fact that there were sometimes calls for the lifting of the arms embargo, and reaction from the FRY, is this an example of such a letter, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. The letter refers, once again, an attempt was made, obviously implying that it was numerous.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If that could be tendered as the next exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit P2463.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You also gave evidence yesterday, sir, and this was at page 31 of the provisional transcript, that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia's mission sometimes made written responses to the Special Rapporteur's reports, and I wonder if Mr. Haider could assist, please, by giving you the 1994 binder. It may be the same binder.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Should be tab E, please.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I have in front of me is, in fact, the 5 August, 1994 report, "Commission on human rights."

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, the document I'm looking at as a title "Note Verbale," midway down the page, dated 28th July, 1994. Sorry it's 65 ter 8835.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [via videolink] We have 8835 here. And that's the 5th, August, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. That's the date, and midway through the page, the first page, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton you are now breaking up, I could not hear that very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'll try speaking closer to the microphone, is that of any assistance?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it is. We are getting interference. That's like a -- not a buzz but it's like a beep, and it seems that it's coming from your end, we've been able to ascertain. It's gone now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It's gone now?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, it seems to be gone. Thank you. If you don't mind repeating your question, we did not hear you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the Registrar to finish with the binder?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [via videolink] We are on 65 ter 08835, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Are you on the first page of that document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were, and it's again Note Verbale.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It's titled "Note Verbale," dated 28th July 1994 from the permanent mission of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And if you could turn the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And you will see at the top of the page there's another title, and it should indicate comments of the government of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia on the sixth periodic report on the situation of human rights, I'm summarising now, submitted by Mr. Tadeusz Mazowiecki; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And if you would -- first, is this an example of the kind of document or written response that you were referring to in your testimony yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Looking at paragraph 1, there's an indication that they are including or attaching as part of their comments --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, at this time I'm going to object to the Prosecution -- I'm getting phenomenal sound in my ears. I don't know if anybody else got that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We are all there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Feedback, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I hope that didn't happen at the New York end. I'm going to object to the Prosecution reading this document. If there is a question to be posed at this point, the Prosecution is describing what the document is and the previous question that -- if this was an example of the kinds of documents that Mr. Sacirbey had seen, I don't know whether or not this is a way of avoiding some of the strictures of the guide-lines with regard to guide-line 27 or not, whether there's some other intent here with regard to what the Prosecution is doing. But at this point, I would make the objection basically on the grounds of leading and testifying.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, what I wish to do is to direct the witness to a portion of the report, read the portion, and then I have a question about the passage I'm going to be asking about and just directing the witness to something that's written in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With that as an understanding, then I'll withdraw my objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, what I was going to direct your attention to is that partway down the first paragraph, the -- there's an indication that also attached are the comments on the part of the report on Bosnia-Herzegovina. And it says paragraphs 5 to 79 of the government of the Republic of Srpska, which I know I didn't pronounce correctly, and my question is, sorry, I'll just have you confirm if you would, if you would turn to page 15 of the document, there should be a section there which says, is titled: Comments of the government of Srpska on aspects of - and I'm summarising - the sixth periodic report. My question for you is whether the Republic Srpska had the right to circulate documents to the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government of the Republic of Srpska did not have recognition and did not have the right to circulate any documents within the United Nations. They may have obviously had the opportunity to communicate with Mazowiecki and other officials of the United Nations on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Under the United Nations protocols, procedures, and rules, was the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia under any obligation to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. I now cannot hear Ms. Bolton through the earphones. I can hear Mr. Sacirbey through the earphones, but I can't hear the questions as they are being made. I can read it, but I can't hear it but there's a some kind of a disconnect. I don't know if anybody else is having the same problem, and now I'm getting the other lovely sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My problem is of a different nature, I hear Madam Bolton not with the earphones very loudly and I don't hear Mr. Sacirbey at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We seem to be having a technical conundrum. I don't know if there is a way of fixing this or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I suggest we break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's take a short adjournment and see if the technicians can help us. Mr. Sacirbey can you say something? Let's see if we can hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I can hear you now. Although there's still the background noise. Madam Bolton, can you say something.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [via videolink] This is the Registrar, we don't have any backgrounds noise at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, it looks like you've transferred your problem to us which you had with the last two days, now we have the background noise now.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [via videolink] Sincerest apologies for that, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: A, B, C, D, E, F, G.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, I hear you there with the background. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you continue your alphabet, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I don't know the rest of.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could you do it again.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: A, B, C, D, E, F, no?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't hear. Fortunately, I can read lips. I've tried it at loud, soft. I've done all of that. Do you mind trying one more time, my apology.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sure. We are testing 1, 2, 3, here on this end. Nothing? Sorry, Mr. Sacirbey, we are having problems. Is there another set of headphones, Mr. Guy-Smith, could try.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm happy to try that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sure this is going to be a very interesting transcript for someone to read where I'm reciting the alphabet. Any luck? 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. I should note that Mr. Harmon was having some problems with his headphones and hearing Mr. Guy-Smith. I don't know if that problem is resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, I'm hearing one of the interpreters in the background which is a gentleman, I believe, is speaking Serbian. But I did not hear Ms. Bolton. This is somewhat like a Philip Glass composition, I think. It's very abstract, but I guess there's some music involved here. If you would be so kind again.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Is that any better?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Again please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Something coming through at all? Sorry, am I coming through at all?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm hearing your voice.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Not through the head phones. I seldom have the complaint, certainly not at home, that people can't hear me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's try Mr. Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... I'm lucky as it is in that people can hear me at home, but here my voice drops.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's see if we can hear Mr. Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Give me the opportunity just to make sure the pronunciation of my name is correct, which is Mr. Sacirbey. Think of being shocked, Mr. Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sacirbey. Thank you very much, Mr. Sacirbey, my apologies for mispronouncing it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I take no offence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. You are very kind. I can hear him very clearly, and I don't have any background noise. I'm happy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I can hear Mr. Sacirbey perfectly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you are still lip reading Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I'm still lip reading Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you want to carry on lip reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'll give it a go. I'll try and see if it works. I'll try and see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Madam Bolton, sorry about that interruption.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, sir. The question I was by asking was whether under a United Nations rules, protocols, and procedures, whether the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was under any obligation to include the RS's comments in its response to the Special Rapporteur?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'd like to go back to discussing the resolution we were discussing at the end of yesterday's session, which was Resolution 819, and you should find that in tab 15F of, I think, the same a binder.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [via videolink] Could Ms. Bolton please repeat --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 819 of the Security Council. We did have it before so ...

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, it may cause you confusion in that the front page, if you will recall, is the report on Resolution 819, it's a letter of transmittal, 65 ter -- sorry, now, it's Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have that. We have that, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And exhibit number is 2462, I believe. And it was, you'll recall, the second page onward of that document. Okay. So the final aspect I want to discuss with you, sir, is numbered paragraph 1 on page 3, and that's the part where the Security Council demands that all parties and others concerned treat Srebrenica and its surroundings as a safe area which should be free from any armed attack or any other hostile act. I want to ask first who sponsored this resolution, if you recall, or this aspect of the resolution, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, it had significant support including from Ambassador Diego Arria, of Venezuela to the French ambassador to the United Nations, Jean Bernard Merrimee. I believe as would probably -- if we had the resolution in front of us, we would see it had very wide support at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: When you are talking about support, is that the same as saying that they sponsored it or proposed it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, I am afraid I don't remember exactly the -- all the countries that sponsored it, but I do remember there were many countries that did, and that it certainly had very wide support, other resolutions, of course, were more contentious.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What was Bosnia-Herzegovina's position on this resolution?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We felt that -- we, that is the mission of Bosnia-Herzegovina and under the instructions of the government in Sarajevo, believed that we needed to do everything and anything that we could to stop the killing at that time, to stop the attack upon the city, and we supported it urgently.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You've told us that your thinking was that this would help, I guess, stop the killing, and that is why you supported it, were there other rationales advanced in the -- well, first, did you raise that issue in the Security Council discussions, either the consultations or any public discussions?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did. Most importantly we raised the issue, of course, in the letters that we forwarded to the president of the Security Council, and in various informal meetings that we had with Security Council members including the none-allying group, which Mr. Diego -- Ambassador Diego Arria was a member of.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I do apologise, Ms. Bolton, but I, perhaps, am behind both you and Mr. Sacirbey with regard to the question, which is the issue at hand being, the resolution itself or the killings that were occurring. There are two potential issues that existed with regard to the questions you asked. I'm not clear as to which issue you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'll clarify.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: My last question wasn't well worded, sir. You've told us what your rationale was for being in favour of this resolution, and what I intended to ask with my last question was whether you shared your reasoning with the Security Council members?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, the concern about the safety and the condition of the Srebrenica citizens and the other refugees in the area was the primary concern, and I think it was, and I'm quite certain it was also the concern of most of those who supported this resolution, and who, in fact, were involved in the debate, as we call it, in the United Nations regarding this resolution.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Other than the rationale concerning the safety and condition of the citizens of Srebrenica, were any other rationales advanced in the Security Council in support of this resolution?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: By who? The question, By who?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm going to answer my friend's question. My question is open on purpose in that I'm asking if anyone was putting forward any other rationale for this resolution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I.e., members of the Security Council, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, if any other rationales were advanced.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, I'm unaware of any other rationale that rose to the level of anything similar to the first priority.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I ask that we move into closed session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: One of the issues that we were discussing in our conversation yesterday was the fact that there had been a delay of voting on a proposed resolution to strengthen sanctions, and yesterday, you identified for us that draft resolution. My question is, was there eventually a vote held with respect to resolution to strengthen sanctions against the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I ask you to turn to the next exhibit in your binder, which should be tab H, and that's Prosecution Exhibit 209, Resolution 820. Do you have that document before you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: At the bottom of the first page, sir, there is a paragraph that begins with the words: "Expressing its condemnation of all the activities carried out in violation of Resolutions 757 (1992) and 787 (1992), between the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Serbian Montenegro, and Serb controlled areas in the Republic of Croatia and the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina." And then continuing on to -- if you turn the page, we are followed by a reference on the next page at paragraph 3 to the fact that there has been a refusal by the Bosnian Serb party to accept an agreement on interim arrangements and the provisional provincial map. What is that agreement and provisional provincial map a reference to?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Vance-Owen Peace Plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, before you go any further, just for purposes of the record, it's a refusal by the Bosnian Serb party to accept not "an" but "the," in its, initial caps, Agreement on; initial cap, Interim; initial cap, Arrangements. So it's identifying a very specific and particular document, which doesn't show up in the record.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. My friend has correctly read out the text.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We'll call it the meat of the resolution seems to start on paragraph B on page 3, which it preceded by the words, "Determined to strengthen the implementation of the measures imposed by its earlier relevant resolutions." And then there's a whole series of paragraphs that followed. The contents of the actual sanctions that are imposed, I don't wish to go into any great detail, but can you just tell us very briefly first, who are they aimed at?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are aimed at ... [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If ever there was an ... [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If ever there was an example of best evidence, this certainly is one. You have the resolution before you. The resident motion is clear on its face. There's no need for the witness to tell us what the the resolution says, to interpret it, or to read or become a reader with regard to its impact, its purpose, or the object of the sanctions contained therein.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour. I can move on to my next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you turn to paragraph 31, sir.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Before you go -- we go on to paragraph 31, why was there a need to strengthen the sanctions?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, excuse me, objection. This particular --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, I will re-word the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Based on the discussions that you were privy to, are you able to indicate what was discussed in terms of the perceived need to strengthen the sanctions?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The failure --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is now calling for a particular interpretation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, I don't hear you now, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I can hear you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is that coming through the microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, you are coming directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm coming directly. Okay. Well, I have an objection, and my objection is that this is now calling for a particular interpretation by the witness as to the perceived need. The witness can testify as to facts, if there are facts that he is aware of. But now we are getting into an interpretation of discussions as opposed to the facts that were discussed, and he is, therefore, rendering an opinion. He has not been qualified for those purposes, and it is inappropriate for him to testify in that fashion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Well, I was an eye-witness to the discussions, Your Honour, and I'm asking him to tell us what was proposed, what were the context of those discussions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess, Madam Bolton, the objection is the use of the word -- is against the use of the word perceived. Maybe if the question was: Based on the discussions that you were privy to, are you able to indicate what was discussed in terms of the need to strengthen the sanctions?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you answer His Honour's question, Mr. Sacirbey, please.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, there was undoubtedly a consensus that the Pale Serbs had, in fact, failed to accept the peace agreement. There was a discussion, to what extent either as a direct party or a direct party Belgrade, in fact, was also responsible for not accepting that peace agreement. A direct party in the sense that they, in fact, would have actually been there to directly encourage, if you would, or direct the Pale Serbs to sign, indirect to the extent that they continued to support the Pale Serbs in view of their failure to accept what was then perceived as a huge chance for peace.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And looking at the text of paragraph 31, sir, under what circumstance did you understand the measures against Federal Republic of Yugoslavia would be lifted?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: At such time that Belgrade and/or Pale, in fact, did accept the peace plan.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I see it is 3.30, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We still have four minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm done with this document and about to move on to another one, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which will take you beyond the four minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we've worked out our technical difficulties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, if we could ask you to turn in you binder to tab 15IJ, please. And this is --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are there, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: This is exhibit already -- Defence Exhibit 31 in these proceedings. You should have before you Resolution 821, Exhibit 31.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, sir, this is resolution, I'll direct you to a couple of passages. It recalls on the first page Resolutions 757, which was the resolution and -- sorry, Resolution 777, which then goes on to say was the resolution that decided that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Serbia Montenegro, should apply for membership in the United Nations and that it shall not participate in the work of the General Assembly. And then turning the page, this resolution goes on at numbered paragraph 1 to reaffirm that principle that it can't continue automatically the membership of the Socialist Federal Republic, and the portion I want to ask you about is that it then goes on it recommend that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia not participate in the work of the Economic and Social Council. What is the work of the Economic and Social Council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is one of the more important bodies of the United Nations. It relates to economic, social, and, frankly, sometimes also political considerations; and, at that time, there was a issue as to whether or not that was covered under Resolution 777.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And how would it affect a state to be excluded from the work of the Economic and Social Council?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, that is outside of the ken of this particular witness's testimony. He is not an expert. He a fact witness. He is now being asked to comment on how something would effect the state, which requires a particular kind of expertise and opinion -- improper opinion testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm asking for the witness to clarify. I can reword it. What advantages, based on his observations and the knowledge of the work that is done by the Economic and Social Council, there may be to having an ability to participate in that work. That's not asking for an opinion, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's a thinly disguised attempt to not ask for an opinion, but it's still asking for an opinion. If it says, What advantages, you know, that makes -- there's a determination made by the witness as to what is an advantage, as to what is not. It's also -- there's -- well, I'll stop there for a minutes, because I know you don't like it when I sequentially engage in objections, I'm going to stop for a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What I don't understand, Mr. Guy-Smith, is this is based on observations and knowledge of the work of this commission or council because he been working -- I suppose because he has been working closely with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't think we've had -- but then we have a lack of foundation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the work that is done by the Economic and Social Council, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did you have the opportunity while you worked there to -- no, that's my foundation question, Your Honour. I don't intend to ask another one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Then, sir, based on your familiarity with the work that's done, your observations, what advantages -- my friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Same objection. Based upon his familiarity, what advantages requires an opinion on his part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But it also --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If he is being qualified as an expert on the functions of the United Nations, if that is what is being sought here, then let's pronounce that as what is going on. If that's not what is going on, then he shouldn't be answering these kinds of questions. And so far, I've allowed a fair amount to go on, but we've been pretty far afield.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You were, maybe I can help --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, there's an objection pending.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Sacirbey. Mr. Sacirbey, when an objection is being dealt with by the Court, you, as a witness, are supposed to keep quiet until the objection is resolved. And, then of course, counsel will direct himself or herself to you. Madam Bolton, I don't know whether you want to lay further foundations for this question that you want to raise or you want to deal with it some other way. It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Maybe you could give us some examples of the kind of work that the Economic and Social Council does?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, I hope I will be responsive. Within the United Nations work, there are various groupings, including something called the Eastern European Group, and the Eastern European Group will, then in fact, have several of its member that will be privileged to directly participate, that is to be a member of the Economic and Social Council. Some other reasons that this resolution, in fact, came up that there was some understanding that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia might even, in fact, become a candidate for the Economic and Social Council. There was also, of course, a view that, in fact, it would participate in other ways in the work of the Economic and Social Council, and, in fact, that this was already prohibited under Resolution 777; but to the extent that that was lacking in clarity, and there was -- there was a view that Resolution 777 was intentionally ambiguous that, in fact, this particular point was to drive that ambiguity out of the question. So that, in fact, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia would not be able to participate in all the economic -- particularly economic and other social political considerations of the work of the work of ECOSOC Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirbey - I see Mr. Guy-Smith is on his feet - but, yes, you are right, you were not responsive to the question. The question was: Could you give some examples of the work that the Economic and Social Council does. If you can just tabulate two, three, four, or whatever number that you can remember of the kind of things that it provided or the work that it did. But before you do so, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour has guided the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I just don't hear you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I said, Now, Your Honour, Your Honour has guided the witness, I was going to be making a different kind of suggestion, but I'm satisfied and there's no reason to go any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay, Mr. Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. As an example, the issue might have to deal with regional economic concerns. That is, some issues of development. Development was a particularly big issue within the Economic and Social Council. That is economic development or something related to economic development. It may also have sometimes to do with the condition of particular population groups. I believe those are probably the best examples that I can provide right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Sacirbey. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no more questions on that exhibit, Your Honour. I did neglect earlier in the proceedings we were discussing 65 ter 8835, and I apparently neglected to ask that it be tendered as an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, this was before the break, early on, and it was the Note Verbale we were discussing from the permanent mission of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. 65 ter 8835, madam, is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2464, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, sorry for the interruption, if you could turn now, please, to tab 15K, you should have the full report of the Security Council mission. The full report is 65 ter 5003 of the, sorry, Security Council mission, pursuant to Resolution 819. Do you have that document, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I want to direct you to certain passages of this document, sir. If you could turn to page 5.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I'm there.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Before I go too far, I should ask what the mandate of this mission was?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was one that, in fact, was given by the United Nations Security Council as a whole to obviously go to the specific locations within Bosnia, but also in the region. And the mission, in fact, did visit Zagreb, did visit Bosnia-Herzegovina, and actually did also stop in Belgrade. And then, of course, to report to the Security Council as a whole and potentially provide recommendations.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. And the composition of the mission, who was part of the mission?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we had the list from before --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. We seem to be falling back into the same problems again here. The document has been admitted. The evidence of who was complemented -- complements the mission is in the document. Best evidence is before us. There is no purpose in having Mr. Sacirbey be a reader unless it's for the purpose of attempting to enhance his credibility. But otherwise, it is absolutely irrelevant for this particular witness to be engaging in this particular function.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess it's only repetitive, not irrelevant. It is Exhibit P2462, you are aware, madam? 65 ter 5003.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I am sorry, you are right. Yes, thank you, Your Honour. That's the correct document. In terms of my friend's objection, I'm trying to not to lead the witness because when I put to him the names of the witness, or I refer the witness to it, he has been objecting on the basis that I'm leading, and if I don't, he is objecting on the basis that it's the best evidence. So I can't win one way or another, but I'll now go to my second way of dealing with it which is to suggest that the list of people who were part of the mission can be found on the first page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Would you agree with that Mr. Sacirbey?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I would, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: One of the members was from Russia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I actually should point out for the Court that I actually flew with this mission to Zagreb itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In terms of political loyalties or alliances in the Security Council, are you able to comment on where Russia's loyalties typically lay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think that question is highly improper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't hear you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Is there something wrong with my connection to Mr. Guy-Smith's microphone?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I said, I believe that the question is highly improper, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you going to tell us why it's improper.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, it calls for an opinion for which there is no foundation. It involves a form of speculation for which there is no foundation, and it takes it -- it places in question an entire can of play of considerations for which this witness has no information we've been presently told about as of yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But the question is are you able to comment on where Russia's loyalties -- Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Loyalties to what? Loyalties to --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I can rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: She's going to rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, based on your observations of dealings with the Security Council, both the public meetings and your knowledge of the informal consultations that took place, when matters pertaining to the conflict in Bosnia arose, who did Russia typically support in those discussions, whose views?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I believe --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. Excuse me. Sorry, Mr. Sacirbey. That assumes, among other things, facts that are not in evidence with regard to views to be taken. It seems to me that what is occurring now is Mr. Sacirbey is being used by the Prosecution as an interpreter of the debate of the conflict between 1992 and 1995, which is not an appropriate function for this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me just say that as I understand ... [Microphone not activated].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not on the microphone. Sorry, can I repeat myself? Rather let me ask you, Madam Bolton, to respond to that objection. Maybe --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm asking the witness for his observations. He is a fact witness. I'm not asking him to interpret anything. I'm asking him to tell us when issues arose, who did -- what views did Russia take and how did those compare to the views taken or expressed by other countries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What are you talking about a specific topic that was being discussed, specific meeting, specific incident?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: No, I'm asking globally what matters. My questions were to global matters pertaining as the conflict in Bosnia arose. And my question was: "Who did Russia typically support in those discussions, whose views?"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think the objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you answer my question, please?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Bolton. The delegation, first of all, I believe, was representative of the full spectrum, and second of all --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm not hearing anything. Was I the only person that couldn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I could hear.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirbey, if you could start again. Madam Bolton didn't hear you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Again, in effort to be responsive, I believe the delegation represented a spectrum of sympathies. And number two, Russia certainly was most sympathetic to the objections that Belgrade authority -- especially as it applied to the issue of sanctions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If I could ask you to turn the page again then, sir, to where we were to page 5. There's a heading "Situation on the ground," a subheading "Srebrenica," and I want to read a few passages or refer you to a couple of passages. And then have some questions for you, okay?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Looking first, sir, at paragraph 7, reads: "Srebrenica, which used to be a spa resort today has a population of approximately 20 to 28.000 people, of whom between 8.000 and 10.000 are locals. The rest are displaced persons from surrounding villages that were destroyed by Serbs. The whole enclave today holds 70.000 people." And then continuing at paragraph 12: "Before the agreement of 18 April, 1993, the town had been under intense shelling. It was surrounded and totally isolated. The situation forced the local Srebrenica authorities to agree to a settlement by which only the Muslim side was to disarm under the supervision of UNPROFOR. That agreement was subsequently concluded by the Bosnian commander, General Halilovic at Sarajevo." Continuing at paragraph 14: "The council should note that when it was discussing Resolution 819 (1993 ), it did not know that negotiations involving the force commander of UNPROFOR had been taking place and that UNPROFOR had participated actively in the drafting and in the process of convincing the Bosnian commander to sign the agreement. The alternative could have been a massacre of 25.000 people." Continuing at paragraph 16: "Srebrenica arrangement cannot be a model but should inspire action by the Security Council to prevent the fall of further enclaves and territories such as Gorazde, Zepa, and Tuzla, which demands immediate action. We know enough today about the conditions prevailing in these towns, notwithstanding Dr. Karadzic's assurance to the mission that his forces would not attack Gorazde or Tuzla." Finally continuing at paragraph 17: "There's no doubt that had this agreement not been reached, most probably a massacre would have taken place..." My first question for you, sir, is: Are the facts that I've read to you consistent with your understanding, firstly, of the agreement -- sorry, let me rephrase. Were you aware of this agreement concluded by General Halilovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only subsequent to the vote of the Security Council. We knew there were discussions going at different levels, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And could you tell me, in terms of this report, to whom -- who would have received copies of this report, sir, within the UN context?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this document was made a document of the Security Council, and, therefore, it would have been, once again, available it to all member states of the United Nations as well as the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, Serbian Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did anyone from your mission or to your knowledge, your government, have any influence over the contents of this report?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that would be accurate. As I said, I flew with the mission to Zagreb, the mission flew thereafter on its own and came back on its own and on authored this report on its own without my input.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: How many missions had the Security Council established of this nature prior to this one?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a rather unprecedented situation, and in my experience, it was the first one that I had seen at that time, in my experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can you comment on how much attention this report was given within the UN context, either the General Assembly, the Security Council, or even in formal discussions between countries?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Once again the wide language of the question is what causes me concern: How many attention, as compared to what? There are no standards that allow for an answer upon which this Trial Chamber can make a reasoned decision in terms of what is being discussed. How much attention? It's a meaningless question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'll rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Was this report the subjects of discussions, sir, in the UN context?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was, Ms. Bolton. And it continued to be for several weeks and months.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And can you comment on whether there was any press coverage of this report?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: How long was the press coverage for?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was extensive and for several days at least. The debate on the issue of safe areas, as you know, continued for several months. Actually, I believe for at least another month.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Brief indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm going to turn to a separate topic now, sir. I'd like you to look at tabs -- first tab L in your binder. And this is 65 ter 8823, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And that should be a letter dated the 4th of May, 1993, from the permanent representative of Bosnia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And it purports, at the bottom, to be signed by yourself. Can you confirm that this is a document you authored?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And just generally related to what was happening in, is it Zepa, Jepa, I know I'm not pronouncing it correctly.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There should be, like, a little sign indicating Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And sorry, is that correct, that's the subject matter of the letter?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If that could be tendered as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Its admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2465, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If you would turn to the next tab in your binder, sir, you should have 65 ter 8825. Do you have a document there, sir, 5th May, 1993? Another letter that purports to have been authored by yourself to the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that in front of me and that is an authentic copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If I could have that tendered as the next exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Its admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2466.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If you would turn, please, to the next tab, sir. Tab NO should have 65 ter 8826.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have that in front of me, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And this is another letter from yourself to the Security Council dated the 6th May, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Is this an authentic copy?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could that be marked as the next exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Its admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document will become Exhibit P2467, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If you could turn to tab R, please, in that same sequence. You should have 65 ter 8829 in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And a letter dated 7th May, 1993. Can you confirm whether you authored this document?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In the second paragraph of this document, there's an allegation that Serbian artillery units arrived yesterday from two towns and took up positions on hills around Zepa. In what republic or what country are those two towns located?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be very clear, we were describing Serbian artillery units that were coming from the region. I cannot confirm to you that, in fact, those were either coming directly from Bosnia or from Serbia proper. Zepa, itself, is on the border of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On which side of the border?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, to try to remember this situation at that time, we were not always sure if, in fact, they had come from one or the other side of the border. We would be very specific --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt. May I interrupt you. The question was --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question was: On which side of the border was Zepa.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Zepa is on the side of the border of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could that be tendered as the next exhibit, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2468, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I ask you, sir, to turn to tab, should be, 10E - sorry - which is in evidence as Exhibit P2443, should be the report of the Special Rapporteur from the 5th May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [via videolink] Ms. Bolton, please confirm the 65 ter number, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, have we located that document or --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe we have. That's the report of the Economic and Social Council, Commission on Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. We've already described this document as having been one of the reports authored by the Special Rapporteur, and if I could ask you turn to paragraph 87.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We have there an indication that: "... massive and repeated violations of the Geneva Convention of 1949 were perpetrated in recent combat in Eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina. They were carried out by Serb forces in Srpska, Konjevic Polje, and Srebrenica, in attacking and ambushing civilians attempting to flee their encirclement, in attacking the villages themselves, in refusing to allow humanitarian aid to enter, and in refusing to allow the evacuation of the wounded, and in attempting to link the above issues to the independent question of freedom of movement for Serbs in Tuzla." And then referring you quickly to paragraph 94C. We have a recommendation that the safe area concept be expanded and applied to other areas of Bosnia and the Special Rapporteur indicates this should immediately be the case with Gorazde and Zepa. My question is, whether that recommendation was discussed at the United Nations Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was, as some of these enclave that are mentioned here actually did fall during that period of time, and the refugees then were concentrated in Srebrenica, in particular, and Gorazde and Zepa to some extent.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can you tell me what the -- Bosnia's position was on this recommendation of expansion of the concept of safe areas?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, at this point in time, we took a contrary view. We believed that if, in fact, only certain sections of Bosnia-Herzegovina, I'm saying we, let me emphasise again for the Court's benefit, this was the view of the government of President Izetbegovic, who communicated to me, as well as the mission of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that the expansion of the safe-area concept to some, but not the whole territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, would, by definition, then leave parts of the country as being unsafe areas and somehow open to continuing attack and abuses. We felt that there needed to be now a comprehensive resolution regarding not only, of course, peace but particularly that moment, the safety of the population. The -- ultimately the designation of just some areas, safe areas, as I said, would leave others as being, in effect, unsafe.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Not withstanding your opposition was the Special Rapporteur's recommendation acted upon by the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Security Council did eventually adopt a resolution with six designated safe areas, and we then proceeded, that is the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Presidency, proceeded to request that, in fact, those methods of ensuring that these are safe areas be firmly outlined; and that, in fact, this would be something more than just a symbolic declaration.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did you ever succeed in getting a firm outline of what those methods would be?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That continued to be a rather dynamic issue. Eventually, NATO was called upon to declare these areas also as protected zones. And to the extent that, in fact, NATO would engage in protecting the civilian population, or, ultimately, as some said, it was only limited to the UN forces within, again that was a rather dynamic discussion.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We'll come back to that issue then, sir. With respect to the fact, you said, that there was eventually adoption of resolution declaring safe areas, can I call your attention, please, to tab 15, I think it's P, which is already in evidence in these proceedings as Exhibit P212, should be a copy of Resolution 824. Could you work off the electronic copy? Is that e-court visible enough to you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was yesterday, maybe we can try that. According to my colleague, the Registrar here, it stops at M. We don't have P in our binders.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I thought we just dealt with R in that same tab?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will endeavour to review what is on screen, and I'll let the Registrar take his time to evaluate what is going on with the documents --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- with the tabs. I cannot see that yet. It's just too far away, and I can try to move closer to the screen. Oh, here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Let me tell you the issue I'm interested in. It may be something you don't need to refer to the document to answer. The resolution --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, if it's of any help and you wish to read something to him because of the situation, I have absolutely no objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What I'm interested in, sir, is that the resolution declared at paragraph 3, the capital city of --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We believe -- Ms. Bolton, we believe we have that. Is this tab 15, it's Resolution 824, 6 May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay, we have that here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Just looking at numbered paragraph 3, we have description of the cities that are being designated as safe areas, and those cities are: Sarajevo, Tuzla, Zepa, Gorazde, Srebrenica, and Bihac. And we've just been discussing what was happening in four of those cities, and I'm wondering if you could comment on the inclusion of Sarajevo and Bihac as safe areas? Could you tell us what, first, was going on in Sarajevo historically at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sarajevo, at that time, had been encircled for approximately, well, actually, at that time, more than a year. It had been denied essential necessities of life, that is from food and water and medicines, and had been under intense shelling and sniping. The civilian population, in particular itself, had been under attack. Bihac is in the north-west part of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is a very significant town, and it had been also surrounded, besieged from several directions, including from the so-termed Croatian Serbs, or the Serbs of the Krajina region of Croatia, as well as the Serbian forces within Bosnia-Herzegovina. The conditions were quite similar to those in Sarajevo in terms of denial of essentials of life as well as military action directed at the population.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can you just clarify by what you meant when you said it was a significant town?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least 100.000 population. And I believe that was inflated by, again, a large number of refugees coming from what is called the Krajina region of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which by then had been largely ethnically cleansed of its non-Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. I want to turn, if I could, please, your attention to the contents of tab 17 in that same binder. The first document there should be 65 ter 8830, a letter from 1st June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have this.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The resolution we were just dealing with was Resolution 824 from the 6th May, 1993. Reviewing the text you have in front of you, and, of course, any independent memory you have, did you recall whether the declaration of those six cities as safe areas brought an end to attacks by the Serb forces in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can you confirm that you authored the letter that's before you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The second page of that correspondence is an annex, that purports to be a letter from President Izetbegovic. Is that who authored this letter, sir?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If that could be marked as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's so marked. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will become Exhibit P2469.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Before we leave this letter, sir, there is an indication by -- in this letter at paragraph 1 that an allegation that the Bosnian Serb forces were reinforced by forces from the Republic of Serbia. Do you have any recollection of where that information came from?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information came from President Alija Izetbegovic. As to his sources, I frankly do not recall that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If you could look at the next document in that same tab, sir. It should be 65 ter 8831. A letter from the 2nd of June, 1993, and this one authored from yourself?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And here you are indicating that you've received an update directly from Gorazde once again, then you set out what is happening. How would you receive information directly from Gorazde at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was possible for the residents and/or the leadership, that is political and/or military leadership, to try to contact us either via telephone or short-wave that would connects into telephone. When I say telephone, I believe in most instances it, in fact, was satellite telephone. I know that they were both -- that is both telephone connections and some short-wave connections. And the contacts were made to my mission, which means that at some times I was actually receiving that information directly, or members of my staff were receiving that information directly.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And finally -- if that could be moved, sorry, Your Honour, as the next exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2470.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Final document on that tab should be 65 ter 8832, sir, should be a letter from the 2nd of June, 1993 from yourself attaching a letter from the president?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And can you just confirm that that is a true copy of the original correspondence?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If that could be marked as the next exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2471.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: With respect to the letters we've been dealing with, certainly the first and second letter, actually all three, you asked that they be circulated as a document of the Security Council. To the best of your knowledge were they circulated?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If we could turn to tab 18, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You should have 65 ter 2184 in front of you, UN Resolution 836.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We've been dealing with the question or the fact that despite the previous declaration of certain areas as safe areas, you've told us attacks continued, and you've documented some of those through letters. And you've also told us that there was a dynamic situation with respect to what a safe area was. Did Resolution 836 clarify to any extent what the UN response was going to be to attacks on the safe area?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if I may just correct; one, I think we all had a pretty good idea what a safe area was supposed to be. The question was: What were the mechanisms by which that would be ensured.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did this resolution address that issue at all?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Looking at paragraphs 9 and 10, there is discussion in paragraph 9 to authorisation for UNPROFOR carrying out its mandate to act in self-defence or acting in self-defence to take the necessary measures, including the use of force, in reply to bombardments against the safe areas. Then at paragraph 10, a reference to member states acting nationally or through region organisations authorizing them to take all necessary measures through the use of air power to support UNPROFOR. The reference to regional organisation, was there any specific organisation or organisations that were contemplated at the time this resolution was passed?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Clearly NATO, the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And from the perspective of your government, based on the wording of this resolution, what were you expecting UNPROFOR and NATO would do if attacks continued on safe areas?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: With the indulgence of the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Sacirbey. Yes, Mr Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: By virtue of some of the testimony we've already heard during this trial, I would appreciate it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you give us a reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would appreciate it if the question asked was not compounds with regard to what UNPROFOR and NATO would do because we have heard from various members of UNPROFOR that their duties and responsibilities were distinct from those of NATO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm actually asking a separate question, which is what his country's expectations were, which is independent of what representatives of UNPROFOR may have testified to in these proceedings as to their understanding of their obligations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. If once again I would ask that the question asked not include both organisations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Split them.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If you could comment on -- if you can comment on those organisations separately?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: At least as the situation evolved, there was what was called a dual-key approach. That, in fact, these two institutions would act in conjunction to an attack upon the safe area. The bigger question, frankly, was under paragraph 9: What did it mean under self-defence. And our major focus was that, in fact, an attack upon the population, in the safe area itself, would trigger response from UNPROFOR and NATO at that time. The two institutions, in fact, that is the UN protection force and NATO, were supposed to act in conjunction, and sometimes that lack of coordination or maybe lack of shared views on the matter, was the one that created the most difficulty in the context of this resolution.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You said that your position was that acting in self-defence included an attack on the population.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Was that view universally held or only held by Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a universal position. At some point in time, the mandate was drawn so narrowly that, in fact, the United Nations Protection Force, itself, would have to say that it was under attack in order to trigger the first key and then the seconds key. The first key being the UN Commanders key; the second key being the NATO Commanders key.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We talked earlier about the fact that -- or some of the rationale that was advanced in terms of the declaration of Srebrenica as a safe area.
