Was the rationale that was advanced for the declaration of these other five cities or towns any different than what had applied to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: In only matters of urgency and time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If I could have -- I think that's not yet an exhibit in these proceedings. Yes, if that could be marked as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 65 ter 2184 is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2472.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, if you could turn to tab 19 in the binder. You should have Resolution 838, which is 65 ter 2183, resolution dated the 10th of June, 1993, from the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I am interested in the second page primarily of this resolution. There is a paragraph that starts with the words "bearing in mind," reference says: Resolution 757, concerning the prevention by all states of imports into their territories of all commodities and products originating in or exported from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia; and a further reference to paragraph 12 of Resolution 820 concerning transshipment; and then numbered paragraph 1 indicates that the Secretary-General is being requested to provide a report on options for the deployment of international observers to monitor effectively the implementation of the Security Council resolutions. Was there any information available to the Security Council that you were privy to -- sorry, what information that you were privy to led to the conclusion or the recommendation that there was a need for deployment of international observers to monitor the compliance with the Security Council resolutions.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually already within the London Conference of August of 1992, there was a call for the deployment of what, here, is called monitors. Actually Bosnia-Herzegovina had been asking for effectively control of the border. Subsequent to that time-frame, there was consistent information that the border, in fact, was being violated, in particular by men and military goods, that is military personnel and goods. And, as I believe, in one of your brief documents, there is -- they had also noted the reports of Mr. Garakan [phoen] who, was the Secretary-General representative on the issue, and who would issue reports to Security Council members. We would sometimes get also -- we would also receive those reports. And if we did not receive them directly, then they would be conveyed to us by member states of the Security Council who would then brief us outside in the UN Security Council anti-Chamber. Finally, there was also, of course, discussion of these points throughout the whole conflict through the sanctions committee of the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Just for clarification, you said in your answer that there were reports of Mr. Garakan on the issue, and what issue were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The issue as a whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Those reports would also include reports by the Secretary-General, generally emanating from the -- presumably emanating from the sources on the ground. With respect to any element of the mandate of the United Nations in Bosnian, everything from, of course, the UN Protection Force to the issue of violations of Security Council resolutions pertaining to sanctions and, in effect, the closing of that border to military personnel and goods.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You have mentioned that information would sometimes come from UNPROFOR on the issue. Were there any other United Nations associated entities before the border -- before this resolution who were tasked with monitoring for violations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There had been present within Bosnia the -- what was then the European Commission Observer Mission they, in fact, may have worked in conjunction with the United Nations. I believe, and this is a very difficult question because we saw them all as coming basically from the United Nations, generally I think what I want to emphasise is the information coming from any UN source was generally filtered through the Secretariat, that is the Secretary-General's office. So we were not always privy as to what was the actual source on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. Was this recommendation that there be monitors acted upon?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I understand it was. Again, the details and the intensity of that were something that was dynamic and developed over time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Were those individuals given a particular title or how would we know who was appointed pursuant to this resolution?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am testing my memory here, but if I'm not mistaken, and I wish to be sure that I'm clear I'm not absolutely sure, I believe, in fact, these individuals did have a separate designation from the UN Protection Force. They, in fact, were called the monitoring mission or something to that degree. I'm -- I believe there's a slightly different title there with the UN word in front of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could that be marked as the next exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so marked. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be Exhibit P2473, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I want to move to a different topic, sir, although we've touched on this briefly, and that is -- and this is again we are still in 1993. We've talked a little bit about the situation in Sarajevo, and I want to ask you about two documents, but we need to ask for a private session for these -- for one document actually, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, we were having microphone problems there, again, Your Honour, but it looks like it's time for the second break in any event. Perhaps we can address the technical issues at the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Bolton. We'll come back at quarter to 6.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: For the record, Judge David is back now, we are no longer sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis. It's a normal session. Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, I think we have only one document left in this binder to discuss, and it should be found at tab 20, 65 ter 6621, Resolution 859 from the 24th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There's a couple of passages I'll refer you to and then I'll have just a few questions. On the first page about halfway down, there's a paragraph that starts with the word "condemning" says: "Condemning, once again, all war crimes and other violations of international humanitarian law, by whomsoever committed, Bosnian Serbs or other individuals." Further on that same page, the Security Council expresses concern about the continuing siege of Sarajevo, Mostar, other threatened cities. Turning the page, if you would, sir, there is then, as underneath the actual resolution section, numbered paragraph 5 where there's a reference to: "Noting with appreciation the Secretary-General's letter, stating that the United Nations has now the initial operational capability for the use of air power in support of UNPROFOR in Bosnia and Herzegovina." Was that air power utilized at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not prior to this date, but subsequent to this date it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can you be any more exact in terms of 1993, can you recall whether, tell me if you can't, whether there was any use of the NATO air power at that point?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were several instances, and the dates would really be now a little bit more difficult for me to remember, although the locations would not be: One of them would be events related to Sarajevo; another one would be to events related to Bihac; a third one, if I'm not mistaken, would be events related to the eastern enclaves, particularly, if I'm not mistaken, around Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can I ask that that be marked as the next exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2474.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, I want to turn to 1994, and as I indicated I think at the beginning of the proceedings, there obviously isn't time to speak about every development in the war, so I want to focus our discussions for 1994 on three areas: First is going to be Sarajevo; second is going to be the commission of experts final report; and the third will be two resolutions from the Security Council. So continuing on the theme or talking about Sarajevo, could I ask you to turn in the 1994 binder -- you have that binder in front of you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Tab A, please. That would be 65 ter 6770, document titled "Note by The President of the Security Council."

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have "Provisional verbatim record of the 3201st meeting of the Security Council."

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: What year is that document you are looking at, sir?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We should have a different binder with 1994, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Court's indulgence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This binder is entitled 1993/1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm told there is a divider, sorry, between the 1993 section and the 1994 section in that binder.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [via videolink] Could Ms. Bolton please repeat the 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, 6770.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [via videolink] Under 6770, Ms. Bolton, I have a document dated the 19th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Court's indulgence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton, are you sure they heard you when you said there was a divider between 1993 and 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, I think I may have the wrong 65 ter number for this exhibit, so I am just going to take a moment and check that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't believe you do. If you do, so do I.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay, well, it's 6770.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [via videolink] That is correct, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Right. Brief indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Can we try bringing that up on e-court. It's not a long document. It's already -- can you see it in the electronic form, Mr. Sacirbey?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can now.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: This is not a lengthy document. In paragraph 2 of this document, let me just refer to you a passage: "The Security Council condemns any hostilities in the United Nations designated safe areas, especially in the Sarajevo area. In particular, it strongly condemns the continuing military pressure on and the relentless bombardment by Bosnian Serb forces of the capital city, Sarajevo. It demands the immediate end to attacks against Sarajevo, which have resulted in a high number of civilian casualties, seriously disrupted essential services, and aggravated an already severe humanitarian situation." And it continues from there. We had been talking in 1993 in August about the situation around Mount Igman. I neglected to ask if that situation had resolved itself by January 1994?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had not. The situation continued to be volatile and militarily active until, if I'm not mistaken, somewhere in the spring of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And this paragraph by the Security Council, does that accurately reflect your understanding based on the information you were receiving from Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And we have discussed this kind of document before, to some extent, and my question is in order -- before a note is issued by the president of the Security Council, is it voted on?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no formal vote. In fact, it does have to be, though, agreed to by consensus.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And is that consensus, does that have to be all 15 members or just the five permanent members or some combination thereof?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Consensus would be all 15 members.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If that could be marked as the next be exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2475.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Under what circumstances would the Security Council issue a statement as opposed to passing a resolution?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Honestly, here was a matter almost of appearance. There had been so many resolutions passed respect of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and some of the resolutions, of course, were repeating --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would beg Ms. Bolton to control the witness when a question like that is asked and an answer like this is given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Guy-Smith. I don't know what you are saying. I don't understand what the basis of your objection is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm just asking Ms. Bolton to control the witness. "Under what circumstances would the Security Council issue a statement as opposed to passing a resolution?" Apart from the fact that I did not jump to my feet to argue that this is, once again, an inappropriate questioning as this particular gentleman because of the lack of foundation, when the response comes as this response comes, this a very specific question. This is an abstract question. And the answer that she's been given clearly does not follow from the question she's asked. She has commented yesterday that she cannot control the witness. She can intercede when this occurs. It is a highly, highly, improper and prejudicial way to proceed during a trial to have a witness run amuck.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection overruled.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, sorry, you were beginning to answer the question that was posed, and just to refresh your memory, you had started to say, "Honestly here was a matter almost of appearance ...," and you were talking about the number of resolutions that had been passed, and if you could just continue if you have anything to add to that?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The resolutions already dealt with factors that were presumably necessary to bring about the desired results. Because the desired results were not being, in fact, delivered, then the presidential statement would be brought about to emphasise the need to comply with previous resolutions or to emphasise acts on the ground that were occurring that were inconsistent with previous resolutions. In the case of Bosnia-Herzegovina there was a unprecedented number of resolutions and, in fact, the Security Council increasingly relied upon presidential statements to recall its previous actions in terms of resolutions to emphasise the need for compliance of those resolutions as well as to bring to the forefront matters, issues, actions that were inconsistent with performance under those resolutions.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to return to January or February of 1994 and events in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could I ask that we move into private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We were talking about a marketplace shelling, and we were talking about a situation in Sarajevo. How was -- what happened or how was the situation resolved in the wake of the marketplace shelling that you've talked about? What happened -- sorry my question is not clear. Strike that last question. What was the situation after February 1994 in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a period there, the shelling was so frequent that probably every other day there were very significant numbers of casualties in Sarajevo from shelling and, of course, continued sniping. When I say significant number, we would have an incident that would cause the death, let's say, of maybe five to ten people, and that almost became an every-day affair as one would put it callously. After this period of time, the heavy weapons began to be, in fact, deposited into containment areas, and in fact, the threat of NATO air action presumably was taken more seriously; and, therefore, the intensity, the frequency of these attacks certainly became less. And even the ability of humanitarian assistance to come into the towns was more frequent. Let me put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We'll clarify this, sir, by looking at a document. If I could ask you to look at 65 ter 5048, which is tab -- that same tab for you. Should be behind the document we were just discussing --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: -- and it's Resolution 900 of the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And there is a reference on the first page of that resolution, in the paragraph that starts with the word "taking note," to a cease-fire agreement of -- reached on the 9th of February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have this.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could you tell us if there was -- you've already started to allude to this, was there any change in the living conditions for the civilian population in Sarajevo following the negotiation of that cease-fire agreement?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, from secondhand reports there certainly was, and from my own personal observations, since I had travelled to Sarajevo before then and after then, there was a very significant change in the -- both in terms of the attacks upon the civilian population as well as the ability of humanitarian assistance to reach that population.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And when we are talking about a very significant change, are you talking about a change for the better or change for the worse?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I was not clear. There was a significant change for the better.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And how long did that improved situation in Sarajevo last?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, I'm being asked to just let you know, as the Registrar here with me, the -- we are hearing you very poorly, but, nonetheless, I can proceed; so just in case we need to ask you to repeat the question, you'll understand why. And to now respond to your direct question, that situation continued until, I think it's fair enough to say, the late summer of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Did there appear to be any particular event that resulted in the deterioration or the -- yeah, the deterioration again of the situation in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was, in fact, a rejection of what then was called a contact group peace plan which was issued to the parties in the early part of that summer in 1994. The rejection came from the Serbian side. By then I should emphasise that the Bosnian government was also representing as the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which, in fact, was a way for the so-called Bosnian Croat party as well as the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina to reach agreement.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. During that period we've just been talking about, roughly February to the end of the summer of 1994, did the incidents of shelling ever stop completely?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not, Ms. Bolton, but frankly as I said, the situation was dramatically different.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And how about sniping incidents, did they end entirely, and I mean by the Bosnian Serb forces in this case?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not. But again it was a very dramatic change.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If this document could be marked as an exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P2476.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I just want to ask you to turn, please, in the binder you have before you to tab H. You should have 65 ter 8836 before you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Should be a letter dated the 15th November, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: In which you are complaining --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, am I screaming back at you? Because as I hear you, as I'm able to hear you less, I might be screaming back or is the volume here at this end okay? I ask you and, obviously, His Honour and Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm able to hear you without difficulty and His Honour is nodding that the volume is all right for him as it is for Defence counsel. You are not shouting at us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If I could just ask again, sir, if you could confirm that this is a letter that you authored?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And again, you asked that it be circulated as a document of the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And again, to the best of your knowledge, was that done?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could that be marked as the next exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that document will become Exhibit P2477.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Turning to the next tab in your binder, sir, tab J, you should have 65 ter 8837. Again, if you could just confirm for me, it should be a letter from yourself dated 17th November, 1994. Could you confirm that you did, in fact, author it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Again it ends by asking it be circulated as a document to Security Council. To the best of your knowledge was that done?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could that be marked as the next exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It is so marked. May it please be given a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P2478, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Madam Registrar. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to move on now from Sarajevo to the second issue that I said I'd like to discuss with you with respect to 1994, and that is the release of the final report from the commission of experts, which you should find at tab B, I think, in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Court's indulgence. It's Exhibit P1536, and I may have the wrong tab. If we could just hold for a minute, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [via videolink] We have it, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And it should be, for the record, I think the first -- the date on it is date of 27th May, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And we have a reproduced -- you should, I think, have pages 1 to 84; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Again, I'm going to refer you to a couple of passages and then I have some questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: If I could refer you first -- I believe there's a cover letter at the very first page, and that is a letter dated 24th May, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have that.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: That's a letter authored, I believe, from Boutros Boutros-Ghali to the president of the Security Council?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Looking at paragraph 4, Mr. Boutros Boutros-Ghali indicates: "On the basis of the information gathered, examined, and analysed, the commission has concluded that grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions and other violations of international humanitarian law have been committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia on a large scale and were particularly brutal and ferocious in their execution. The practice of so-called ethnic cleansing and rape and sexual assault, in particular, has been carried out by some of the parties so systematically that they strongly appear to be a products of a policy, which may also be inferred from the consistent failure to prevent the commission of such crimes and to prosecute and punish their perpetrators." Was this letter received by yourself?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was, Ms. Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And the text of the actual report?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did review the report.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: And is that a document that you had to seek out?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm just looking for the document right now, and I was going to see if it was made a document of the Security Council. I don't see that designation, but we did receive this report, and I do remember it very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Looking at the first page of the document, of the letter we were discussing, there's letterhead that looks like Security Council, does that mean anything in terms of its circulation?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was noting that because it shows it as distribution general, which means the general membership. And it appears to be a document of Security Council. What I didn't see is the Secretary-General anywhere asking for it to be distributed as such, which I guess he didn't have to, it was distributed as such.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. If I could refer you to paragraph 129, which is page 33 of the English version. At paragraph 129 in the first section of it, there is discussion of the term "ethnic cleansing" in both -- they are citing from an interim report. And we had been discussing earlier in our exchange whether there had been a definition of ethnic cleansing ever adopted by the Security Council. Can you tell me, was there agreement as to whether this is the definition of ethnic cleansing?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe this comes as close as there is to consensus.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Looking at paragraph 131, there is a reference with respect to the practices by Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it then says: "Ethnic cleansing is commonly used as a term to describe a policy conducted in furtherance of political doctrines relating to Greater Serbia?" Can you assist us in what those -- when we have reference to the political doctrines, what is that a reference to?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is in reference, in particular, to the very broad notion of Greater Serbia. That notion was applied with the strategy, plan, if you would, of incorporating any area that was deemed to be somehow a part of the territory that Serbs did or had occupied to be part of, in effect, a redefined Serbia, an enhanced or expanded Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Brief indulgence, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ms. Bolton, it really is extremely annoying, the noise that we are getting at this end. So please excuse me that my concentration is being rattled.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Are you able to hear me clearly, sir, or is it such that you can't understand what I'm saying? Are we breaking up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm able to hear you with quite great concentration, so my answers are, to some extent, distracted by the focus on hearing you. Continue, I'll try to do the best that I can here.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: You are breaking up a little bit on this end but not too badly. Just a moment, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Registrar in New York suggests maybe we take a short break and try to re-establish connection.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay. We are going to try to re-establish, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a short break. We will be called. --- Break taken at 6.31 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton, had you got an answer to your question or had you --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I just want -- can you hear us now, sir, or how are things on that end?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are about the same, maybe even slightly worse, but as I understand, it's for another 15 minutes, and I'll try to maintain my concentration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton, if I may just interrupt --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: -- given the noise in the background, if we adjourned now, would everybody be available to sit tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: The problem is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We cannot hear, Your Honour

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I am sorry, I guess my suggestion has just been shot down.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Three in the morning is a little early for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Three in the morning is a little early. What I said was, Could we switch tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't have any problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, no, but tomorrow morning, it will be 3.00 in New York, 3.00 in the morning, so we can't sit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honour, I'm willing to be here. I'm willing to be here if I can be allowed to come into the building. I will not object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's the problem, I don't know whether the Registrar next to you there or Madam Corominas would be willing to be there at 3.00 in the morning, so I would hate.

utterances.speaker: MS. COROMINAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Madam --

utterances.speaker: MS. COROMINAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Madam Corominas here, that would be fine with me to be here at 3.00 in the morning. The building is open.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is the building open? And Mr. Registrar?

utterances.speaker: MS. COROMINAS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Let's check out with the people here then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- having lived for awhile as a child in New York, I know that New Yorkers are tough people, and you know, they can stay up all night. But I'm not sure that this is necessarily an effective way of doing things, because if we have a transmission problem tomorrow, I don't know whether all the rest of the staff that's involved in the technical aspects of this particular kind of video transmission are also going to be available. I think we need to make sure about that too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's actually what the Registrar was raising with me, and it does look like it's logistically a little difficult to arrange a sitting tomorrow morning. We may just have to adjourn to another date.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I agree. I agree, I have no difficulty with adjourning to tomorrow, Your Honour, and I think there would be a number of logistical issues with trying to start at 3.00 in the morning, New York time, including the fact that we haven't booked the time for the videolink for that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Aren't we scheduled to sit in the afternoon tomorrow anyway?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: We are sitting in the afternoon tomorrow, starting at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay, well, why don't we postpone until tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Somehow I had it in my mind that something else was happening in the afternoon. Sorry. Okay, then let's adjourn to tomorrow. This time it will not be half past 2.00, it will be quarter past 2.00. Is that okay? Courtroom I for people in the Netherlands, right where you are there in New York. Mr. Sacirbey, I must warn you again, you don't talk to anybody until you are excused from testifying -- talk to anybody about the case. You can talk to other people, to everybody about anything else. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I believe I heard Your Honour's -- Your Honour's words. I believe I have heard them correctly and has to do with me speaking to anyone else regarding the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Sacirbey. Have a good day and we'll meet tomorrow. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
